options: Magnesium, 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s²
Sulfur, 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁴
Silicon, [Ne] 3s² 3p²
Carbon, 1s² 2s² 2p²

why.correct: One peak per subshell, with height = number of electrons: 2 + 2 + 6 + 2 + 2 = 14 electrons, silicon.
options: Magnesium has four subshells, so four peaks; this spectrum has five.
Sulfur's lowest-energy peak would be 4 electrons tall, twice the 3s peak.
Right: peak heights 2, 2, 6, 2, 2 add to 14 electrons.
Carbon has three peaks; this spectrum has five.

items.q: Which subshell gives the peak at 10.3 MJ/mol?
options: 2p
2s
3p
1s

why.correct: Read from high to low binding energy in filling order: 1s (178), 2s (15.1), 2p (10.3), 3s (1.46), 3p (0.79). The 6-electron height also marks a p subshell.
options: Right: it is the tallest peak (6 electrons) and the third from the left, after 1s and 2s.
2s holds 2 electrons; the peak at 15.1 MJ/mol is 2s.
3p is the outermost subshell, at the lowest energy (0.79 MJ/mol).
1s is closest to the nucleus, with by far the highest energy, 178 MJ/mol.

items.q: Why is the 1s peak at a far higher binding energy than any other peak?
options: 1s electrons have more charge than the other electrons
The 1s subshell holds the fewest electrons, so each is held more tightly
1s electrons are the valence electrons, which are the most tightly held
They are closest to the nucleus, with no shielding electrons

why.correct: Binding energy reflects Coulombic attraction. The 1s electrons are nearest the nucleus and are not shielded, so they feel nearly all 14 protons.
options: Every electron has the same charge, −1.
Peak height (number of electrons) does not set the binding energy; distance and shielding do.
The 1s electrons are core electrons; valence electrons are the most loosely held.
Right: least distance and no shielding give the strongest Coulombic attraction.

items.q: Which electrons in this atom are its valence electrons?
options: The electrons in the tallest peak
Those in the two lowest-energy peaks
The electrons in the peak with the highest binding energy
The six electrons at 10.3 MJ/mol and the two at 15.1 MJ/mol

why.correct: Valence electrons are in the outermost shell (n = 3 for silicon): the 3s and 3p peaks, 4 electrons in all.
options: The tallest peak is 2p, a core subshell; height shows the number of electrons, not their role.
Right: the 3s and 3p electrons are in the outermost shell, the most loosely held.
Those are the 1s core electrons, the most tightly held.
Those are the 2s and 2p core electrons in shell 2.

items.q: Every peak in magnesium's spectrum is at a higher binding energy than the matching peak for sodium. Which explanation is best?
options: Magnesium has more electrons, which pull each other closer to the nucleus
Its extra proton pulls harder on each subshell
Magnesium atoms are larger, so their electrons are held more tightly
Magnesium's electrons are in higher shells than sodium's

why.correct: Coulomb's law: more protons (12 vs 11) pull harder on electrons in the same subshell, so every binding energy rises.
options: Electrons repel each other; the extra pull comes from the extra proton.
Right: same subshells and similar distances, but a larger nuclear charge.
Larger distance would mean weaker attraction; and magnesium is in fact smaller.
Both atoms fill the same shells, 1 to 3.

items.q: How do the lowest-energy peaks of the two spectra differ in height?
options: They are the same height, since both are 3s peaks
Sodium's is taller, since sodium loses its electron more easily
Magnesium's is six times as tall, like its 2p peak
Magnesium's is twice as tall: 3s² against 3s¹

why.correct: Peak height is proportional to the number of electrons in the subshell: 1 for Na 3s, 2 for Mg 3s.
options: Same subshell, but height counts the electrons in it.
Height shows the number of electrons, not how easily they are removed.
Only the 2p peak is 6 electrons tall.
Right: Na 3s¹, Mg 3s².

items.q: Using the spectrum, what is the minimum energy needed to remove one electron from one mole of gaseous sodium atoms, in kJ/mol?

mistakes.why: Value: that is the 1s electron, the hardest to remove. The minimum energy removes the outermost (3s) electron.

why.correct: The most loosely held electron is the 3s electron, with a binding energy of 0.496 MJ/mol. 0.496 MJ/mol × 1000 kJ/MJ = 496 kJ/mol.

items.q: A student predicts that aluminum (13 protons, [Ne] 3s² 3p¹) will have a new small peak at a binding energy just above magnesium's 3s peak. What is wrong with the prediction?
options: Aluminum should have no new peak, since it fills the same subshells as magnesium
The new peak should be 6 electrons tall, since it is a p subshell
The new 3p peak belongs below aluminum's 3s peak, at lower binding energy
The new peak should be at a higher energy than aluminum's 1s peak

why.correct: Aluminum keeps magnesium's four peaks (all shifted to slightly higher energy) and adds a 3p peak of height 1 at the lowest binding energy, below its own 3s peak.
options: Aluminum adds a 3p electron, a new subshell, so a new peak appears.
Height counts electrons present: aluminum has one 3p electron.
Right: a new p subshell appears at the far right, at the lowest binding energy.
1s is always the most tightly held; a 3p electron is far less so.

items.q: In photoelectron spectroscopy, what does the height of a peak tell you?
options: How tightly those electrons are held
The number of protons in the atom
The number of electrons in the subshell
Which shell the electrons are in

why.correct: Position = binding energy (how tightly held); relative height = number of electrons in the subshell.
options: That is the peak's position along the energy axis.
The atom's protons shift every peak; height counts electrons.
Right: more electrons ejected at that energy give a taller peak.
The shell is read from the position and order of peaks.

items.q: A spectrum has three peaks with relative heights 2, 2 and 5. Which element is it?
options: Fluorine
Phosphorus
Boron
Neon

why.correct: Add the heights for the total: 9 electrons, fluorine.
options: Right: 2 + 2 + 5 = 9 electrons in 1s, 2s and 2p.
Phosphorus has five subshells, so five peaks.
Boron is 1s² 2s² 2p¹, with peak heights 2, 2, 1.
Neon's 2p peak would be 6 electrons tall.

items.q: Which statements about photoelectron spectra are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Each peak corresponds to one subshell
A larger nuclear charge shifts matching peaks to lower binding energy
Electrons in a 2p subshell have a higher binding energy than those in 2s
The peak with the lowest binding energy belongs to a core electron

why.correct: Peaks map to subshells; more protons raise every peak. 2s lies above 2p in binding energy, and the lowest peak is always valence.
options: Right: all electrons in one subshell share one binding energy.
More protons pull harder on every subshell, so matching peaks move to higher binding energy.
In one atom, 2p electrons are held a little less tightly than 2s: lower binding energy.
It belongs to the outermost (valence) electrons.

items.q: Put the subshells of argon (1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶) in order of binding energy, highest first.
options: 1s
2s
2p
3s
3p

why.correct: Binding energy falls as electrons are farther out and more shielded: 1s > 2s > 2p > 3s > 3p.

items.q: Compare the spectrum of potassium (19 protons, [Ar] 4s¹) with that of argon (18 protons). Predict the change from argon to potassium.

variables.name: Binding energy of the 1s peak
variables.why: One more proton pulls the 1s electrons harder.

variables.name: Number of peaks
variables.why: Potassium adds a 4s subshell: six peaks instead of five.

why.correct: One more proton raises every matching peak; the new 4s electron adds a new peak of height 1 at very low binding energy.

items.q: In a photoelectron spectrometer, how is the binding energy of an electron found?
options: By weighing the atom before and after the electron leaves
By counting how many electrons leave each second
From the size of the atom measured under a microscope
Light energy minus the ejected electron's energy of motion

why.correct: The light supplies a known energy. Part of it frees the electron (the binding energy); the rest becomes the electron's motion, which is measured. Subtracting gives the binding energy.
options: An electron is too light for its loss to be weighed this way, and mass is not energy here.
The count gives peak height, not binding energy.
Atoms are far too small for that, and size does not give the energy directly.
Right: whatever energy is not used to free the electron stays with it as motion.

items.q: Two peaks in one atom's spectrum are at 1.46 MJ/mol and 0.79 MJ/mol, with equal heights. Which statement is supported?
options: The electrons at 1.46 MJ/mol are held more tightly
The electrons at 0.79 MJ/mol are closer to the nucleus
The peak at 0.79 MJ/mol has more electrons
Both peaks belong to one subshell

why.correct: Binding energy measures how tightly an electron is held: 1.46 MJ/mol is held more tightly than 0.79 MJ/mol. Equal heights mean equal numbers of electrons.
options: Right: a higher binding energy means more energy is needed to remove them.
Closer electrons are held more tightly and have the higher binding energy.
The heights are equal, so the numbers of electrons are equal.
One subshell gives one peak; two positions mean two subshells.
